passages.title: Tennis Scoring System
passages.resource: Despite its complexity, the tennis scoring system has been stable since the Victorian period. The modern game of tennis traces back to a medieval game called jeu de paume, which began in 12th century France. It was initially played with the palm of the hand, and rackets were added by 16th century. With its strong association with pageant traditions of the French court, Wilson says, tennis was highly stylized from the beginning. Over a course of the next few centuries the game saw periods of incredible popularity, with more than 1,000 tennis courts in Paris in the 16th century. Though it's well known for being beloved among royalty (Henry VIII was a notable and avid player, and the French revolutionaries' tennis court oath was made on an indoor court at Versailles), it was also enjoyed among commoners and monks.

questions.questionText: The game of tennis traces back to the Victorian period
questions.answeringReason: The passage states the modern game traces back to jeu de paume, a medieval game originating in 12th century France — well before the Victorian era. Only the scoring system is described as stable since the Victorian period.

questions.questionText: The ability to initially play with just the palm of the hand made it appealing to commoners
questions.answeringReason: The passage confirms commoners enjoyed the game, but gives no explanation as to why. We cannot assume the palm-playing mechanic was the reason without the passage stating it.

questions.questionText: Tennis has held on to the same characteristics since its inception
questions.answeringReason: The passage states the game 'was highly stylized from the beginning' and that its scoring system has been stable since the Victorian period, supporting the idea that its core characteristics have been retained throughout its history.

questions.questionText: Jeu de Paume was played with a racket
questions.answeringReason: The passage states rackets were added by the 16th century, but it is unclear whether this was while the game was still called jeu de paume or after it had evolved further. We cannot confirm or deny the statement from the passage alone.

passages.title: Chocolate Aroma
passages.resource: After a few moments, Cat signals to let go of our noses. Whoosh! As the aroma molecules waft from my mouth to the back of my nose, they fire the nerve signals that tell my brain about the different compounds in the chocolate. Suddenly there's a flood of flavors: rich chocolate, a little bitterness, some bursts of fruitiness. And just when I think the flavors are fading, I detect a wave of something else. Is it coffee? "You can see that a lot of the subtlety of the flavor of chocolate is in the aroma," Cat says. By some estimates, only 10 to 20 percent of what we perceive as flavor comes from our taste buds — the rest is delivered through our nose. Cat has the kind of covetable job careers advisers never tell you about at school. A chocolate expert and judge in international chocolate competitions, Cat also lectures at the International Institute of Chocolate and Cacao Tasting (IICCT) in London — and she is teaching us how to taste chocolate like professionals.

questions.questionText: "The subtlety of the flavor of chocolate is in the aroma" is most likely to mean
questions.answer: To experience the different nuances of the taste, you must smell the chocolate
questions.answeringReason: Cat's statement emphasises that the subtle, nuanced aspects of chocolate's flavour are carried through the aroma rather than the taste buds alone. This is best captured by option 2 — experiencing nuances requires smelling the chocolate.
options: To experience the different nuances of the taste, you must smell the chocolate
Some flavours can only be experienced after smelling the food
In order to fully enjoy the chocolate one must experience the aroma

questions.questionText: The author thinks that Cat's job is:
questions.answeringReason: The author describes Cat's job as 'covetable' — meaning highly desirable or envied. This is most accurately expressed as 'sought after'.

questions.questionText: How many flavours are mentioned as existing in the chocolate the author tasted?
questions.answeringReason: The author explicitly mentions three flavours: rich chocolate, a little bitterness, and bursts of fruitiness. The possible fourth (coffee) is presented as a question, not a confirmed flavour.
The passage directly states: 'aroma molecules waft from my mouth to the back of my nose'. This clearly identifies the direction of travel.
options: The back of the mouth to the nose
